abstract: As a visitor, and one not wishing to trespass on the subject of electric light and power supply schemes for small-sized towns in South Africa, I would only like to draw attention to the extraordinarily good results produced by some members of your Institution with regard to the use of wood-power gas. I know very excellent work was done in Australia, and, during the war, we had five large stations — ammunition works — on wood. I wish to record my extreme interest and appreciation in visiting one or two wood-power factories here, particularly the one at the Leeuwpoort mine, where, I think, a change over from coal to wood in the producers was beneficial. They had one specially designed wood producer from Australia, and afterwards converted the standard Campbell producers to wood.

articleTitle: An introduction to the study of electric traction in natal
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Engineers in South Africa, and doubtless in other countries also, have looked forward to an authoritative account of the electrification of the Glencoe-Maritzburg section of the S.A. Railways. It is eminently satisfactory that this task has been undertaken by an engineer so well qualified to deal with it. The synopsis presented by Mr. Pask succeeds admirably in outlining the main features of the scheme; and the engineering profession is fortunate in being promised a series of papers which will cover the various sections of the work in detail. The bold initiative shown by the Railways and Harbours Administration in embarking on what is, for a, conservative country, a scheme of daring magnitude was bound to enlist the benevolent interest of the engineering profession at large, and of electrical engineers in particular. I feel I am on perfectly safe ground in saying that none will rejoice more heartily than the electrical engineers to see the scheme in Natal a complete success from both the technical and the economic points of view. The superiority of electric traction in handling heavy freights over steep gradients is so well established that a fairly large capital expenditure can usually be justified, provided only that a sufficient volume of paying traffic can be secured for the line. In the case under review there appears to be every reason for believing that the line will in due course receive as much traffic as it will be able to handle.

abstract: Mr. W. H. Badger raises the question of the comparatively short life which corresponds with the ordinary catalogue rating, but it must be remembered that catalogue load figures were calculated on formulae based on the Stribeck and Goodman investigations referred to in the paper, and that the original Stribeck and Gcodman formulae or variations of them are still largely used for this purpose. The recent investigations which developed the kinetic rating demonstrated the life which corresponded with certain loads, and 1,000 hours' life was found to correspond with certain makers catalogue ratings. The 10th part of this, viz., 100 hours, is a convenient duration for a laboratory test. Further, the late A. W. Macaulay showed in his paper, “The Endurance of Ball Bearings with special reference to Automobile Practice,” read before the Institute of Automobile Engineers in May, 1923, that the catalogue rating was sufficient to ensure a satisfactory life in six out of the 19 positions in which ball bearings are customarily fitted in a motor car, and recommends a factor of 1 to 1·5 for eight of the remaining positions.

articleTitle: The use of ball and roller bearings in electrical machines
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: From the day when the cup and cone ball bearing was found to make such an enormous improvement in the efficiency of the bicycle, the use of ball and roller bearings in industrial machinery has increased by leaps and bounds. The motor car was developed after the engineer had learnt to appreciate the ball bearing, and, in consequence, there has never been any real difference of opinion between Automobile engineers regarding the comparative merits of plain and rolling type bearings. To a large extent industrial machines were designed and running comparatively satisfactorily on plain bearings before the industrial engineer had extended more than a passing interest to the ball bearing. In consequence, the growth of the use of the new type of bearings in general machinery has been slow, and, in many classes of machine, the first ball or roller bearing was applied only when the makers failed to make a plain bearing do the work to their satisfaction. In other cases pressure has come on the manufacture from customers, who, finding a solution to their bearing troubles in converting them to the rolling type, have refused to consider machines equipped with plain bearings when making purchases.

abstract: I have first of all to. thank those members of the Institute who showed sufficient interest in the paper to discuss it, and, first of all, I deal with the President's appreciative remarks, in which he criticises the system we have of placing transformers in pits in the footpath, and says he can see no objection to the concrete transformer kiosk placed above the road level. Unfortunately, however, we have other people than ourselves to please, and, though I might not see any objection either, we have a Borough Engineer in Durban who raises all sorts of objections to our sub-stations, and we are literally driven underground in finding accommodation for transformers. I specially mention this because in the May-June number of the Metropolitan-Vickers Gazette is an article on static sub-stations in urban and suburban areas, in which is illustrated an arrangement almost identical with ours, with the pits in the footpath and switch-gear in a cast-iron pillar adjoining. There is also illustrated another device similar to ours in a steel tank, used where a brick pit cannot be drained, this tank being also placed underground with its switchgear in close proximity in a pillar.

articleTitle: An introduction to the study of electric traction in natal
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: On April 13th, 1926, the final section of the Maritzburg-Glencoe Electric Traction Scheme was made “alive,” and on April 18th, 1926, the section was handed over to the Traffic Officials, and electric traction instituted on freight and passenger trains as a matter of regular routine. The time is, therefore, opportune for a review of this great engineering undertaking, and, in fact, has been demanded by students of electric traction in South Africa and abroad. The subject is, however, too big to be condensed into the time allocated for an evening's discourse, and the plan adopted, which, it is hoped, will commend itself to members, was to edit a series of exhaustive papers on each of the various sections of the work, viz., Power Station, Transmission Lines, Track Equipment, Sub-stations, Switchgear, Locomotives, etc., which have been prepared with the help of the sectional engineers, and from these to write a synopsis of moderate length.
